en: The meaning is: "by Kapila, Kaṇāda, Gautama, and so forth, as well as by their disciples, up to the present day.

The meaning of "recollection of an author" (*kartṛsmaraṇa*) is: a traditional remembrance (*smṛti*) that makes known the fact of having an author. Now, one might object: since no one has directly perceived the Lord, the speaker of the Veda, at the beginning of creation, there would be no recollection due to a lack of experience.
If it is argued that in the absence of that [Veda], the composition of the sages' Smṛtis would not be possible, we say no;

for by means of the inference of its being of human origin, one perceives a speaker of the Veda, and thus the composition of the Śruti and Smṛti based upon him is possible. Otherwise, regarding the Veda...

Regarding the non-acceptance of the Veda having an author: in that very context, within the Smṛtis themselves, he demonstrates not only the Śruti but also the Smṛti regarding the Veda’s having an author—starting with the words "In this way. Now, an objection:
surely the Mahābhārata and other texts that teach the eternity of the Veda are themselves the proof for its lack of an author.

He raises the doubt that [it] "will come to be"—that is, [the word] *svayambhū* means "eternal. The phrase "this Blessed One" (*eṣa bhagavān*) is also a qualifier of the Veda. As for the claim that [it is] "mere praise," in that case, due to the contradiction with the previously cited Śruti and Smṛti, this Bhārata would not have its own literal meaning as its intended purport (*tātparya*).

The sense is that [the text] is intent upon praise. "Because of the possibility of error and so forth" means because of the possibility of defects such as delusion and negligence in a person. "By virtue of being eternally omniscient" means by virtue of possessing knowledge whose objects are all things eternally.
"Because of being faultless" means because of being devoid of delusion and the like. "Precisely for this reason" means precisely because of the absence of eternal omniscience.

[Objection: Why not simply accept that the Veda possesses eternal faultlessness rather than being composed by an eternally omniscient person, and let that alone be the ground for the Veda's authority? In this way, the inference of its having an author would be sublated. To this, he states the refutation of the Veda’s eternity with the words "Furthermore" (kiṃca).
"Of that composition" means "of that specific sequence residing therein.

The point is that if the sequence were eternal, then because it would be eternally inherent in something non-eternal, the sequence would necessarily result in being a *jāti* (universal). And in this context, [the definition of a word] consists in being the object of the will of a reliable person, which takes the form of being the object of the will of God (*īśvara*).

Since a purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason exists even in the case of eating *kalañja* (forbidden food), and since the probandum— in the form of being a means to a desired end qualified by not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—
is absent there, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). How, then, can that [reason] be an inferential indicator for it?

If the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) were an intention characterized by the property of being a means to a desired end qualified by not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, then—due to parsimony (*lāghava*)—let "being a means to a desired end not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" alone be the meaning of the optative; what is the use of an intention? This is the underlying dissatisfaction expressed by the phrase "the teachers, however... (*ācāryās tu*).

This has been indicated. The objection that "let the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) be [the fact of being] desired, so what is the use of [positing] 'being a means to a desired end' (iṣṭasādhanatva)? is indicated by the words "it is not so" (*na tv iti*). Now, it might be argued that the understanding of "being a means to a desired end" cannot arise from the injunction because it is contradicted in the case of sacrifice—that is, the fact of being a means to a result qualified by the nature of heaven (*svargatva*) is absent in sacrifice, as [heaven] is produced by such acts as bathing in the Gaṅgā.

If it is argued that this is not so because of deviation—since, although the sacrifice possesses the status of being a means (sādhanatva) characterized by a specific uncommon property (vaijātya) residing in heaven, that specific property cannot be known prior [to the performance of the act] as it must be postulated through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the injunction’s teaching that heaven is the goal to be achieved; and thus, it is impossible to grasp the power of the injunction with respect to a causality defined by such a property—then we say: no.

Some maintain that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely a causality (*kāraṇatā*) consisting of a specific relation of essential nature (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Others hold that being the cause of heaven consists in being a state that possesses a property which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its necessary posterior existence, where that delimiting factor is not a delimiting factor of the locus of "otherwise-established" status (*anyathāsiddhi*). But in reality:

The causality of heaven consists precisely in possessing a property that serves as the delimiting factor for the invariable antecedence determined by the property of being heaven delimited by dharma; and this is not sublated in the case of sacrifice with respect to that which is delimited by the property of "heaven-ness," which is the form of a specific universal (vaijātya) residing in heaven.

Because there is no deviation [in the cognition]. Now, an objection: even if the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*) has the power (*śakti*) to denote being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), how can there be a cognition from it of its being a means to heaven (*svargasādhanatva*)? If one were to postulate distinct powers for each—such as being a means to heaven and so forth—there would be an infinity of powers (*śaktyānantya*). Nor [can it be argued that this is unnecessary] because [the meaning] is already present through the injunctive suffix...

It might be argued that because the heaven presented by the word *svarga* is construed non-differently with the object of desire (*iṣṭa*), the understanding of "being a means to a desired end that is non-different from heaven" is possible; however, this is not so, because since the word *svarga* is contained within a compound, its meaning cannot be construed elsewhere. If this is raised, we say: no.
Because the understanding [of the injunction] is accomplished by postulating the injunctive power (*śakti*) with respect to being a means to heaven and so forth;
nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for the understanding of each individual [element],
since [the specific nature of the means] is dependent upon the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "heaven" and consists of those respective properties.

This is because the grasping of that very [intention] serves as the decisive factor. Nor does this entail an infinity of verbal capacities, since we accept a single capacity with respect to the means-hood as determined by properties such as "being heaven" (*svargatva*). Furthermore, there is no difference in capacity based on the difference in the delimiters of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), because [the property] functions as the delimiter of desirability (*iṣṭatāvacchedaka*).

This is because, having made "being heaven" (*svargatva*) and so forth the common property, one accepts a single denotative power (*eka-śakti*) with respect to the instrumentality (*sādhanatva*) as determined by that [property]. Nor should it be argued that heaven-ness and the like would appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) only as the delimitors of desirability (*iṣṭatāvacchedaka*) and not in their own form (*svarūpataḥ*); for "being the delimiter of desirability" functions merely as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Because a qualifier is the object of the word's expressive power (*śakti*), it is accepted that only the qualifier appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, being a mere adventitious indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) consists in not being the object of the cognition produced by that word despite being the object of its expressive power, whereas being a qualifier consists precisely in being the object of the cognition produced by that word while being the object of its expressive power.
The status of being a qualifier has been explained more extensively elsewhere [in verse 150]. Regarding the phrase "of the inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇasya*):

it refers to the ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) directed toward that material cause (*upādāna*), which consists of the inherent cause of that [object], with respect to the purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) aimed at accomplishing that [object].

It is not the case that activity aimed at producing sound would not occur in the case of a drum and the like, because its material cause (upādāna), space (*ākāśa*), is beyond the reach of the senses; nor should it be said that activity aimed at producing destruction would likewise fail to occur, because its inherent cause (*samavāyin*) is unestablished. For this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

This is because, according to the ancient view, only a volition directed toward another that is to be accomplished by the direct perception of sound is admitted as having the drum and so forth as its object. However, in the new view, it should be understood that the mere locus [of the sound] is the material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, in the case of sacrifices and the like, the oblation is the [material cause] of the word.

It should be understood that for the movement of breath and so forth, the flute and other instruments, as well as the channels (nāḍīs) through which the breath flows, serve as the material causes (upādāna).

In the root text, the phrase "due to aversion" is stated with the intention that aversion directed toward the result and the cognition of it as a means to what is disliked are the instrumental causes (karaṇa) for cessation. [151] As for the phrase "for the movement of breath indeed..."

The meaning is as follows: the movement of breath, such as excessive breathing and so forth, is accomplished through effort; it is observed to be accomplished by perceptible effort, because one observes an increase in the act of breathing upon an intensification of effort in one who is running.
"And thus" means: when the illustrative example has been established. "Of all" refers to [the case] in one instance.

The sense is that since the fact of being achievable through effort is experienced, by means of that example, one can infer—by way of the delimiting condition of being a movement of the vital breath—that such movement everywhere is produced by the effort of an enjoyer. That very [effort] is what is inferred as the cause of the movement of the vital breath. However, the Neo-logicians (navyāḥ) hold it to be the effort that originates life (jīvanayoni-yatna).

There is an absence of proof [for the existence of a soul], because the activity of the vital breaths can occur through a contact between the self and the mind caused by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) conducive to life, or rather through an unseen force that is not the cause of that [activity];

furthermore, the aforementioned inference is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Otherwise, [if it were conclusive], one could [falsely] infer [the existence of a soul] in a single effort, using the example of its being produced by knowledge.

They say that because it would follow that effort produced by cognition must be considered as being produced by cognition in all cases delimited by being produced by effort, it would further follow that even cognition and so forth—which are beyond the senses—must be postulated during deep sleep. || 152 ||

The property of "not being the non-inherent cause of falling," defined as being distinct from that which is the inherent cause of falling, is over-extensive (ativyāpta) in the case of color and other qualities;
therefore, he explains it as "the non-inherent cause. He adds "first" because the second and subsequent instances of falling have velocity as their non-inherent cause. And thus:

The point is that gravity is established by the following inference: "An action occurring at a time when conjunction is not present has gravity as its non-inherent cause, because it is an action, like an action produced by conjunction.
[153, 154, 155] Regarding the phrase "produced by conjunction with fire":
The meaning is that it has conjunction with fire as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
He says "accompanied by oiliness" (*snehasahita*) to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that will be mentioned later. And that [oiliness] is exclusively natural (*sāṃsiddhika*).
Thus, because the causality is based on being natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatvatva*), there is no inclusion of the fluidity of gold and the like.

This is the intended meaning. Nor should it be argued that, since there is no over-extension [of the definition] simply by taking viscidity (*sneha*) as the cause [of cohesion], there is no evidence for the fact that natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) is the cause of cohesion;
for, given the absence of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the causality resides in the property of viscidity or in the property of natural fluidity, both must be accepted.

Because it is the cause [of the destruction of fire]. (156) This oiliness perceived in the oil is watery; it resides in the water-component contained within the oil. If that were the case—namely, if the oil admitted the presence of a water-component within it—it would follow that it is antagonistic to fire, which entails the destruction of the fire. [This is] with respect to the destruction of fire by means of conjunction.

The sense is that it is because water is the cause [of the action]. (157) Regarding the statement "velocity is produced": velocity-ness (*vegatva*) is a specific universal (*jāti*) established through perception. As for the word "by that": since at that time there is no subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*) which could destroy the action, it is velocity alone that acts as the destroyer of the action.
The sense is that it is "conceived" (*kalpyate*). "From that" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the destruction of the prior action.

"And so on hereafter" (*evam agre 'pi*) means that by the subsequent action as well, there is the destruction of the previous momentum (*vega*), and from that, the arising of another momentum; such is the general direction of the argument. Without... [text truncated]

And [the phrase] "and momentum" (*vega*) means that without momentum, the destruction of action would not occur; this is the sense, because there is no other cause for destruction. Now, one might ask: "What is the harm if there is no destruction of prior action? To this he says: "And the production of action would not occur. The reason for this is [stated in the following verse regarding] action.

Regarding the phrase "because of being an obstacle": here some [opponents] argue that since the destruction of the previous action and the production of the subsequent action can occur through the subsequent conjunction alone, there is no purpose in accepting the destruction of the previous action and the production of the action by means of that [conjunction]; therefore, momentum (*vega*) is redundant. Thus, by means of momentum...
They say that perception itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding velocity, because [the object] "goes" by virtue of generating an action. Regarding the phrase "of further going":
the meaning is "of the action that produces a conjunction as it did previously."

The point is this: because elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) is what is to be established [by the reason], velocity (*vega*) produces an action that generates a conjunction with a subsequent location, but it does not produce an action that generates a conjunction as it was before;
therefore, elasticity is not rendered superfluous by velocity.

Elasticity (*sthitisthāpakatva*) is established as a specific genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being the delimiting property (*avacchedakatā*) for the production of a specific kind of action. Furthermore, elasticity is that which produces a specific action, is destroyed by the action it itself produces, and is imperceptible (*atīndriya*); this has been stated almost entirely in the root-text (*mūla*). And thus: [159] (Note: The phrase "And thus" (*itthaṃca*) indicates that the following point follows logically from the preceding definition.)

And regarding the prevention of memory through equanimous cognition (*upekṣājñāna*) in the manner described, he states "furthermore" (*kiṃca*), asserting that in reality, the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) lies precisely in the fact that equanimity and other types of certainty (*anyaniścaya*) serve as causes for the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). This is because the postulation of a [separate] impression would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
The phrase "the state of being a cause for memory itself as non-ascertainment of another [object], through equanimity," and so forth;
the connection of the subsequent ablative ending (*pañcamyantam*) in the word *siddhatvāt* is also with the word *na*. ||160||

It should be understood that because the word expressing the subject (uddeśya) is required first, this [word] "this" (asau), which refers to the object (uddeśya), is placed before [the verb] for the purpose of demonstrating its grammatical connection (anvaya). In that context, it is with regard to the mental impression (saṃskāra); therefore, the mental impression is postulated.
Alternatively, let the destruction (dhvaṃsa) of the experience itself be the operation (vyāpāra),
because the principle that "the counter-positive and its absence produce a single cognition" is not a necessary determinant.
Nor should it be argued that this would result in the experience becoming an obstacle (pratibandhaka) to memory.

Because the meaning of the term "obstructiveness" (pratibandhakatva) is precisely the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as the locus of a causality delimited by the nature of a relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāvatva), and because in this case there is no causality by virtue of being a relational non-existence;
and because remembrance is possible in the third moment through a mental impression (saṃskāra) produced in the second moment following the experience.

It should not be argued that the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) cannot function as an operation because the destruction of the experience does not exist prior to the result [of remembrance]; for even in that case, remembrance is admitted to occur only after a moment's delay. If this is said, we reply: no, because if mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) were not accepted, there would be no remembrance at any time of what was previously experienced.
Because the operation consisting of the destruction of the experience would always exist, since it [the experience] is always present;

nor should it be argued that there is no recollection due to the absence of an awakener (*udbodhaka*), for in a case where five or ten recollections of a jar or the like have occurred through an awakener in the form of the cognition of a specific object, but no more than that—

In the recollection of a jar or similar object, since the cognition of that very object is the determinate awakener [of the latent impression], it is impossible to assert the absence of an awakener when that [object] exists. In reality, however, it should be understood that the establishment of the latent impression (saṃskāra) is beyond dispute by virtue of the reasoning proving the "unprecedented" (apūrva) which will be stated immediately hereafter.
Because causality is impossible if either its own activity or [the activity of] another is absent at the moment immediately preceding the production of the effect;
for the definition of causality consists precisely in being that which possesses either its own activity or the activity of another at the time-point immediately prior to the effect.

[The word] "bhāvaḥ" [means] "because it is not the cause. This means that being produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not the determining factor for something being a memory. He presents the view of the author of the *Maṇi* with the words "But others [say]...
According to your own position, regarding the manifestation of memory that must be postulated in the interval, the awakened latent impression...
In my view, however, the postulation of its being the cause in recognition is the same as the postulation of its being the cause in the manifestation of memory;
and this is the same whether one postulates the manifestation of memory as an intermediate step or postulates its being the cause in recognition itself.

By the statement "your respect [for this] is excessive," a lack of conviction is indicated. Regarding the phrase "heaven and so forth" (*svargādi*), he demonstrates that the word "heaven" (*svarga*) includes mere pleasure, while the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the body, the sense organs, and the rest—this is shown by the passage beginning with "all [the fruits] such as heaven" (*svargādisakala*).
Below...

The same applies here as well regarding "hell and so forth" (verse 161). In that context, regarding "dharma," the term "sacrifice and so forth" includes, by the word "and so forth," burnt offerings (*homa*) and gifts (*dāna*). Sacrificality (*yāgatva*) consists in being a desire whose qualificandum is a particular substance characterized by the destruction of one's own ownership, directed toward a deity. Being directed toward a deity means having as its qualificandum something characterized by the ownership of a deity. [This is because] the deity is composed of sound (*śabdamayī*).

In this context, however, "objecthood" (uddeśyatva) consists in being the object of a superimpositional cognition such as "this belongs to that. "The nature of an oblation" (homatva) is the state of being an activity such as pushing [the ladle] and so forth, which resides in ghee and the like, and which is conducive to an action conducive to conjunction with fire.
And "the nature of a gift" (dānatva) [consists in giving] without the taking of a price.

The traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*) holds that sacrifice (*yajña*) is the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) which causes the destruction of one's own ownership and the production of ownership in another.
Others maintain that sacrifice-ness (*yāgatva*), oblation-ness (*homatva*), and so forth, are specific universals (*jāti*) cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
In that regard, the *śrāddha* rite is a sacrifice from the perspective of the ancestors, whereas it is a gift (*dāna*) from the perspective of the Brahmins.
Others say that this is not tenable because it leads to confusion (*sāṅkarya*). Otherwise, there would be an absence of dharma;
for even an experience that has long since perished could produce memory. Therefore, he says: "by way of being devoid of activity" (*nirvyāpāratayā*).

[He says] "long destroyed": [this refers to] an action (*karman*) that has perished over a long period of time, which [would otherwise lead] to a fruit without an intermediate excellence (*atiśaya*), namely the *apūrva*.

The meaning is that it is not capable, i.e., not able, to produce the result. Such being the case, since there is no capacity for both the destruction and its counter-positive to be the producer of a single effect, only one *apūrva* (unseen potency) is postulated.
In reality, however, even the destruction of the sacrifice is not the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*); for if that were so—

In order to prevent the production of heaven from a sacrifice that has been defiled by *kīrtana*, the exclusion of *kīrtita* (defiled) must be included within the defining scope (*avacchedaka-koṭi*) of the causal capacity for producing heaven;
however, since there is no single such property as "being *kīrtita*," it is impossible to include a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by "being *kīrtita*. Therefore:

In the case of the individuals mentioned [in the scriptures], only a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the respective individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) should be introduced. And thus, in the case of the ten sacrifices mentioned, since there exists a mutual difference between those respective individuals,
a heap of differences (*bhedakūṭa*) alone must be introduced in order to prevent the production of heaven.

The status of being a delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) must be accepted. In that case, due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, there would be an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations. However, if one accepts the "unseen force" (*apūrva*), since sacrifices are proclaimed to be momentary, their conjunction is impossible; thus, [the various] differences must be subsumed within a single locus.

There is an absence of purpose; for at that time, there is no absence of a specific instance of sacrifice delimited by those differences [of the Veda] such that a transcendental result (*apūrva*) would have to be produced from the recitation of such [a specific Veda]. Nor should it be argued that the placement of the recited Vedas in a single location is necessary by virtue of their connection with the *apūrva*.

Since heaven would be impossible without the production of an *apūrva*, the aforementioned distinctions are not included within the category that delimits the generative capacity for heaven; likewise, because the aforementioned sacrifice has perished, they are not included within the category that delimits the generative capacity for destruction.
"Because it is impossible for that which has been stated to be included within the divisions"—this is a path not yet explored by others.

Regarding the phrase "in the state of being a cause": the meaning of the locative case is "being a constituent. The same applies further on. "Just like existing at the time of the effect": as in the case of the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) regarding its causality.

The meaning is that existing at the time of the effect (*kāryakālavṛttitva*) is a constitutive factor [for the status of an instrument], but this is not the case for the causality of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, by means of such things as the destruction of the ritual act (*karmanāśa*) or touching the water of the Karmanāśā river; "of that" refers to the sacrifice and so forth;
"prior" means prior to the destruction of the ritual act, the touch of the Karmanāśā water, and so on; "because it has occurred" [is the reason].

The meaning is "because it has arisen and because it has perished. The point is that since the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a capable and all-pervading substance (*yogya-vibhu*) are destroyed by the qualities produced immediately after them, a sacrifice consisting of desire perishes at its very third moment; this applies to what follows as well. Regarding the phrase "dharma decays" (*dharmaḥ kṣarati*), [the meaning of] *dharma*...

It is not correct to say that because sacrifices and the like "perish" (kṣarati) and thus do not become the enjoyer of the fruit, it is logical that the contact with the waters of the Karmanāśā river and so forth acts as an obstacle to the fruit such as heaven by means of the relation of self-destruction (svadhvaṃsa). [For] after one Aśvamedha sacrifice, there is another Aśvamedha.

If it is argued that [the performance] has already been completed (*kṛta*), then subsequently, even upon performing an *aśvamedha* sacrifice, the undesirable consequence would follow that heaven (*svarga*) does not arise. Nor should it be said that because the act of proclaiming it (*tatkīrtana*) acts as an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) toward that which is defined by the nature of heaven produced by that specific *aśvamedha*, there is no possibility of heaven arising from another *aśvamedha*.

When the glorification (*kīrtana*) of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is performed, since the attainment of heaven resulting from that sacrifice is not established [at that time], it is impossible to postulate such a relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*). Furthermore, that *apūrva* (unseen potency) in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is of two kinds: the ultimate *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*) and the intermediate *apūrva* (*kalikāpūrva*). To explain:
When the cake on eight potsherds for Agni becomes unfailing on both the new-moon and full-moon days,

he performs the Upāṃśu sacrifice between them; with those two, they offered this cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma at the full moon, and curd for Indra at the new moon, and [curd] for Indra [at the full moon].

From the six [sacrifices], beginning with the Āgneya, which are enjoined by the five sentences such as "payo 'māvāsyāyām" (milk on the new moon day), there arise six originary apūrvas; these alone are called the *kalikāpūrvas*, and from them arises the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*). Now, it may be asked: are not the six apūrvas necessarily required?
If it is argued that the sacrifices themselves should be the direct causes of heaven, what is the need for a supreme *apūrva* (unseen potency)? This is not so;

for by the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," it is understood that the means to heaven is that which is delimited by both [the new- and full-moon sacrifices]. Since a single operation must be postulated for that which is delimited by both, there is no room for intermediate *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-potencies).
Because it is not produced by that which is delimited by both [the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa],

and because at the time of the operation of the injunction "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa," only a single apūrva is postulated as the mediating function (*vyāpāra*) for the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa, which have long since perished; and it is not the case that, immediately thereafter, there are six...

In the cognition of the sequential order of sacrifices, there is the conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) of postulating six *apūrvas*, because that [complexity] is justified by its resulting fruit.

Nor should it be argued: "Let the supreme *apūrva* be produced by five [sacrifices] through the medium of five *apūrvas*, and by the sixth sacrifice directly; what is the use of a *kalikāpūrva* for the sixth?"

Since the supreme apūrva (transcendental result) is produced only through the cooperation of the sixth [sacrifice] with its subsequent auxiliary and sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the sixth sacrifice does not persist for that duration; therefore, an apūrva produced by it is necessarily required.
In this regard, with respect to the supreme apūrva and with respect to heaven, [the cause] is that which pervades the states of being a *darśa* and a *pūrṇamāsa*.

Some maintain that the causality [of the sacrifice] consists in the common genus (*sāmānyajāti*) shared by both the New Moon (*darśa*) and Full Moon (*pūrṇamāsa*) sacrifices. Others hold that the causality resides in the specific forms of "New Moon-ness" and "Full Moon-ness," such that the production of the result occurs through their conjunction, like a staff and a wheel.
In this view, a single *apūrva* produced by the three-fold *darśa* sacrifice functions as the mediating operation for the three *kalikā-apūrvas*. Thus...

Some maintain the position of nine *apūrvas* as follows: a single *apūrva* is produced by the full-moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), which consists of three parts, and this [single *apūrva*] has the three *kalikā-apūrvas* as its intermediate operations (*vyāpāraka*). From those two [the full-moon sacrifice and the new-moon sacrifice], there arises the *apūrva* that produces heaven; and that is called the "supreme *apūrva*" (*paramāpūrva*) or the "*apūrva* having the fruit as its head" (*phalaśiraskāpūrva*). It is in this very context [that they speak].
Others hold that there are eight *apūrvas* because there is no evidence for an *apūrva* possessing a fruit (*phalaśiraska*).

The moderns (*navya*), however, maintain that there are only seven *apūrvas* as previously stated, since the supreme *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*) can be accounted for by the six *kalikāpūrvas* alone, and there is no evidence for the two intervening *apūrvas*. This...
Some maintain that in rites such as the *jāteṣṭi* and the *pitṛyajña*, an unprecedented [apūrva] arises residing in the agent;

however, the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*) holds that it resides in the enjoyer. The Prābhākaras, on the other hand, assert that the sacrificial action does not perish in its entirety, but rather persists in a subtle form within those elements that initiate the body for the attainment of heaven.

They say that [the result] begins to arise by abiding either in the substances that constitute the sacrificial act or in the self who is the performer of the sacrifice. That is not so; for since the sacrifice, consisting of cognition, desire, and so forth, is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self, it is necessarily restricted to not persisting beyond four moments.

This is because knowledge, desire, and so forth are never perceived simultaneously [with their substrates], and it is therefore accepted that they are destroyed by subsequent qualities residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Otherwise, by such a logic, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the entire world would always exist in a subtle state. Enough with this elaboration. ||162||163||
[Objection: But why is it that dharma and so forth do not arise in God through the sight of the Gaṅgā and other such things?

To this he says: "But these two [dharma and adharma] are produced by latent impressions (vāsanā). The sense is that because God lacks the latent impressions produced by false knowledge, there is no arising of dharma and so forth in Him. [Objection: But...
Since there is no evidence for the claim that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the cause with respect to merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*), he says:
"In the *Muktāvalī*, therefore. [This refers to] one who possesses knowledge—that is, one who possesses the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
"Because of the contradiction with his statement" means that, according to him, experience [serves only] for the mere destruction of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

The meaning is: "because of the demonstration of its being the cause. "And thus" means: "and when [it is established that] karmas are destroyed only by experience. "Otherwise" means: "in the absence of its being indicative.
"All karmas" means: "all unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by karmas. [The text says: "he reduces them to ashes."

It destroys [the notion of permanence]. Having shown the Smṛti, he shows the Śruti: "And they perish," which has that very intention—namely, the intention regarding *prārabdha* (commenced) karma. Regarding the phrase "due to prolixity" (*gauravāt*):
it refers to the postulation of multiple instances of the word "darśa," their respective prior non-existences, and the causal relations between them.

The meaning is "out of respect. (Verses 164, 165, 166). "Because of contradiction with the aforementioned cognition" means because of the contradiction with a cognition characterized by arising and perishing. "And in this way" means if recognition has as its object something belonging to the same class. "Of both" means...
The meaning is: "for the sake of establishing production, non-perception, and recognition. On this point, the Mīmāṃsakas argue:

through the recognition that "this is that very same letter *ga*," the persistence of the letter *ga* and others over that duration is established as the object [of cognition]; since there is no destruction by any intervening sound or other factors, and because there is an absence of any cause for destruction, the eternity of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is proven.

Furthermore, recognition does not have "belonging to that same class" as its object, because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. Otherwise, if it were so in all cases, the consequence would be the destruction of non-difference.
Nor is the superimposition of contradictory properties in the form of intensity and dullness a subverting factor, given the force of recognition.
Since its permanence is established, it is postulated that qualities such as high pitch (*tāratva*) belong to the manifesting air;

thus, there is the possibility of perceiving even the high pitch and other qualities of the air by means of the auditory organ. That which is high in pitch is the very same thing that is low in pitch relative to something else.
They say that this is because there is no contradiction between the intensity and the mildness of perception. That is not correct;

for if that were the case, since properties such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) and *gatva* (the quality of being *ga*) would also result in being attributes of the manifesting air, the distinction between the phonemes *ka* and *ga* would not be established, leading to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that all phonemes are identical. In reality, however, according to the position that phonemes are non-eternal...

In the view that phonemes are eternal, the property of being *ka*-ness (*katva*) and so forth is the delimiting factor of the effect for the impacts of the throat, palate, and other articulatory organs; however, in the view that phonemes are eternal, the property of being a direct perception of *ka* (*kasākṣātkāratva*) is the delimiting factor of the effect for those same impacts.

Because of complexity. Nor should it be argued that even under the view of eternality, the property of being a *katva* (the universal of *ka*-sounds) alone is the delimiting factor for the effect-ness (*tajjanyatāvacchedaka*) by way of worldly objectivity (*laukikaviṣayitā*), and thus there is no room for complexity;
for this would result in the failure to include the perception of a "kolāhala" (a tumultuous noise). Indeed, the perception of a kolāhala...

Otherwise, by the same logic, since the production of a jar and so forth would have "being perceived as a jar" (*ghaṭapratyakṣatva*) alone as the delimitor of its effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), that [production] too would necessarily be eternal.
Furthermore, under the view that [the jar] is non-eternal, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has as its object the fact of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*).

It must be stated that [the cognition] would be "this belongs to that class" (tajjātīyaḥ ayam), but not "this is that" (so 'yam). For it is accepted that in a case of recognition where the universal (jāti) such as the phoneme *ga* appears as a universal, the form of the cognition is "this belongs to that class," whereas in a case where it appears in its own specific nature (svarūpataḥ), the form is "this is that."

In this regard, the following should be understood: sound is of two kinds—consisting of resonance (*dhvani*) and consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). Among these, with respect to the first sound produced by conjunction, which consists of resonance, the ether (*gagana*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and the conjunction between the drum and the ether is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
The contact between the drum and the drumstick, and so forth, is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
However, with respect to the first sound, which consists of a tone produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-dhvani*),
the disjunction between the space and the bamboo-split is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), while the disjunction between the two halves of the bamboo is the efficient cause.

The efficient cause (*nimitakāraṇa*) [is as follows]: with respect to the first sound, which consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), the conjunction of the ether (*ākāśa*) with the throat, palate, and so forth, is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); the conjunction of the throat, palate, and so forth with the air (*vāyu*) and other elements is the efficient cause (*nimitakāraṇa*). However, with respect to the second and subsequent sounds...

The word "first" refers to the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the conjunction of the drum with space or the conjunction of the throat and so forth with space being causes of sound;
for, by the rule that every positive effect is necessarily produced by a non-inherent cause, their status as such causes must be accepted.
However, in the absence of evidence for such a restriction, let there be no causal status for those [atoms],

since the production of sound is possible through space alone, assisted by instrumental causes such as the conjunction of a drum and a stick; and in the case of the first sounds and so forth, [this occurs] precisely through their own effects, which are subsequent sounds.
The destruction of the final [moment] occurs either through the penultimate sound or through the destruction of the penultimate sound.

In the root text, the phrase "that very same medicine," etc., includes such examples as "this is that very same lamp-flame. But surely, even in those cases, there is simply no difference between the individuals?
Therefore, he clarifies the meaning of the word "bhāva" (the object) with the passage beginning, "The medicine which was prepared by me," and so forth.
And here, there arises a cognition of difference produced by the superimposition of two contradictory properties: namely, having oneself as the agent and having an agent other than oneself.

The sense is that because of the presence of an obstructing factor, the non-difference of the individual is not the object; rather, the object is the non-difference of what belongs to the same class as that [individual]. || 168 ||

Having bowed to Bhānu and having reflected upon the essence of the scriptures, this *Muktāvalī-prakāśa*, which was assigned by his father, has been brought to the path of illumination by this Sun-like [author] with the rays of his own sound reasoning; may it be for the delight of the wise. *Muktāvalī-prakāśa*.
May Nīlakaṇṭha, the beloved of Satī, attain satisfaction through this [work], which is the sun that destroys the darkness of one’s own ignorance.
Thus ends [the work] composed by the illustrious Dinakara Bhaṭṭa, son of Mahādeva Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of Bālakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa— the full moon in the ocean of the lineage of the venerable Bhāradvāja.
The exposition of qualities in the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalīprakāśa is concluded; and this work is finished.

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence."
